questions.q: This lesson's first extraction question is "who said this, and what are they actually experiencing?" What does it illustrate with Harrow's VP of Sales?
options: The VP's sentence compressed three different segment leads' specific frictions into one vague complaint
The VP of Sales is always the most reliable source of requirements
Only executives should be interviewed during requirements extraction
The VP's complaint required no further investigation
questions.explain: The VP didn't experience the specific frictions directly — three segment leads did, each with a different concrete problem. Finding the person closest to the actual pain is what the first extraction question is checking for.

questions.q: What is a "solution disguised as a requirement," per this lesson's example of "move to Salesforce Field Service"?
options: A stated, checkable need that any design can be verified against
A named mechanism presented before the underlying need (e.g., stop double-booking technicians) has been separately stated, foreclosing alternative designs
An assumption the stakeholder explicitly confirmed
A requirement that has already been fully satisfied
questions.explain: Naming a specific technology before stating the underlying need separately forecloses evaluating whether that technology is actually the right fit — the underlying requirement (stop double-booking, stop certification mismatches) could in principle be satisfied by more than one approach.

questions.q: How does this lesson define an assumption, as distinct from a requirement?
options: An assumption is always false by definition
An assumption and a requirement are the same thing once written down
An assumption is something a design relies on without explicit confirmation from the stakeholder, while a requirement is a stated, checkable need
Only requirements can appear in a design document; assumptions never should
questions.explain: A requirement can be verified true or false against a design. An assumption is something the design quietly depends on that hasn't been explicitly validated with the stakeholder — which is exactly why it should be surfaced and checked, not buried.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say separating requirements, assumptions, and named solutions on paper matters for a design review?
options: It eliminates the need for stakeholder sign-off entirely
It has no practical effect on how a review goes
It is only useful for documentation purposes after a project ships
It lets a reviewer challenge an assumption or question a named solution's fit, while treating the actual requirement as the one thing that shouldn't move without stakeholder agreement
questions.explain: Keeping the three categories distinct lets a reviewer push back on an assumption or a named solution's fit without accidentally re-litigating the underlying requirement itself, which is what keeps a review focused and honest.

questions.q: Renwick's original ask was "one portal" for two different audiences. What assumption did this lesson say was hiding inside that sentence?
options: That one undifferentiated experience would work for both audiences, which turned out to be wrong and costly once challenged
That Experience Cloud could not support more than one license tier
That partners and customers should never share any technology at all
That no sharing mechanism of any kind would be needed
questions.explain: "One portal" implicitly assumed one license tier and one experience would serve both audiences — an assumption that, once surfaced and tested against each audience's actual task list, turned out not to hold.
